schema_notes: Each heuristic: id, category, scope, applies_when, platforms, title, trigger, check, good_example, bad_example, default_severity, default_finding_type. Optional: notes (author-only, not sent to model).
authoring_principle: Designer-shown, not engineer-implemented. Every finding must be actionable by adding or changing something visible in the design. If the fix lives in code, the heuristic does not belong here.

scopes.screen: Applies to a single uploaded screen. The most common scope.
scopes.flow: Applies across multiple screens. Activated when ≥2 screens are uploaded and form a sequence.
scopes.intent: Compares the design against the PRD or context provided. Activated when a PRD/context is uploaded.

finding_types.gap: Directive. The state/element is provably absent and the design needs it. Voice: 'Add X.' / 'Mock Y.' / 'Design the Z state.'
finding_types.recommendation: Suggested improvement with a clear better answer in most cases, but room for legitimate disagreement. Voice: 'Consider X.' / 'We recommend Y.'
finding_types.question: Subjective or context-dependent observation where the designer may have made an intentional choice. Voice: 'Is there a reason X?' / 'What's the intent behind Y?'

heuristics.title: Skeleton state matched to content shape
heuristics.trigger: A screen shows content fetched from a server: lists, feeds, dashboards, profile pages, content cards, search results.
heuristics.check: Has the designer included a skeleton frame that approximates the eventual content layout (rectangles where text/images will be)? Or is the loading state missing entirely / replaced with a generic centered spinner?
heuristics.good_example: A feed of posts has a skeleton frame in the design file: greyed rectangles approximating the avatar, header line, and 2–3 body lines per post.
heuristics.bad_example: No loading frame in the file. The designer only mocked the populated state, leaving engineering to invent the loading experience.

heuristics.title: Designed failure state for optimistic UI updates
heuristics.trigger: A user action immediately updates the UI before the server confirms — liking, favoriting, adding to cart, marking as read, sending a message, toggling a switch.
heuristics.check: Has the designer included a frame showing what the UI looks like when the optimistic update fails? The reverted visual + the error feedback (toast, inline message) + the retry affordance.
heuristics.good_example: The design file includes: (1) liked state with heart filled, (2) failure state with heart reverted and a toast 'Couldn't save your like — Retry'.
heuristics.bad_example: Only the optimistic-success state is in the file. The failure path is missing entirely, so engineering has to invent what reverting looks like.
heuristics.notes: Highest-value catch in the library. Designers nearly always design the optimistic path and skip the rollback.

heuristics.title: Designed progress UI for operations longer than ~2 seconds
heuristics.trigger: An action triggers a server operation that can reasonably take more than 2 seconds: file uploads, exports, AI generation, batch operations, large search.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn the progress indicator (bar, percentage, step counter, time estimate) and a cancel affordance? Or is the long-operation state left as a generic spinner with no progress signal?
heuristics.good_example: Upload state in the file shows a per-file progress bar with bytes/total, an estimated time remaining, and a cancel button per file.
heuristics.bad_example: Long-running action has no designed progress UI — just the same spinner used for quick loads. Engineering has to invent what 'in progress' looks like.

heuristics.title: Visible indicator for background data refresh / new data available
heuristics.trigger: A screen displays data that refreshes automatically in the background (live feeds, dashboards) OR where newer data may arrive while the user is on the screen.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn a visible indicator for when a background refresh is happening (e.g. 'Updating…' badge in header), and a designed affordance for 'newer data available' (e.g. 'X new posts — click to load')?
heuristics.good_example: Feed design includes a 'Updating…' indicator in the header during refresh, and a 'View 3 new posts' pill that appears at the top when new data is available.
heuristics.bad_example: Refresh behavior is mentioned in the PRD but no visible indicator is designed — engineering picks a UI pattern or omits the indication entirely.

heuristics.title: Designed in-flight state for user-initiated actions
heuristics.trigger: A user clicks/taps a primary action — submit, save, send, add — that triggers a network request.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn what the action looks like while it's in flight? Disabled button state, loading-spinner-in-button, label change to 'Sending…'? Or is the in-flight state missing?
heuristics.good_example: Design file includes the 'Send' button in three states: default, in-flight (disabled with inline spinner, label 'Sending…'), and after-completion.
heuristics.bad_example: Only the default state of the button is designed — what it looks like during the request is unspecified.

heuristics.title: Distinct designed empty states: first-time vs. user-emptied
heuristics.trigger: A screen displays a user-owned collection that could be empty: cart, inbox, saved items, notifications, projects, drafts, files.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn distinct empty states for (a) a first-time user who has never added anything and (b) a user who has emptied/cleared a previously populated collection?
heuristics.good_example: File includes two empty-cart frames: first-time ('Your cart is empty — start shopping' + 'Browse Products') and emptied ('Your cart is empty — view recent orders or continue shopping').
heuristics.bad_example: Only one generic 'No items' empty state in the file. The two situations look identical, missing the chance to orient or re-engage.

heuristics.title: Designed empty state for filtered or searched lists
heuristics.trigger: A list or grid supports filtering, sorting, or search.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn a distinct empty state for when filters/search return zero results — clearly attributing the empty result to the filter (not the underlying data) and offering to clear filters or broaden the search?
heuristics.good_example: Filtered-list-empty frame in the file: 'No products match these filters' with a 'Clear filters' button and a 'Try removing Brand X' suggestion.
heuristics.bad_example: Filtered-empty state isn't designed separately — it falls back to the generic 'No items here yet', confusing the filter case with a truly empty list.

heuristics.title: Designed search-no-results state with the search term echoed
heuristics.trigger: A screen has a search input over a content corpus.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn a no-results state that echoes the search term, offers spell-check / 'did you mean' alternatives where possible, and suggests broadening criteria or browsing instead?
heuristics.good_example: No-results frame: 'No results for "wireles headfones". Did you mean "wireless headphones"?' with the suggestion linked, plus a 'Browse categories' fallback.
heuristics.bad_example: Search-no-results state is the same generic empty state used elsewhere, with no echoed term or recovery suggestion.

heuristics.title: Designed empty state for permission-restricted views
heuristics.trigger: A screen shows resources whose visibility depends on user permissions or role — team projects, organization data, restricted folders.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn a distinct state for when the user lacks permission to see content (vs. when content truly doesn't exist), with an explanation and a path forward (request access, contact admin)?
heuristics.good_example: Permission-restricted frame: 'You don't have access to projects in this workspace. Request access from your admin.' Visibly distinct from the no-content-yet frame.
heuristics.bad_example: Permission-restricted views aren't designed — they fall back to 'No projects here', identical to a truly empty workspace.

heuristics.title: Every designed error includes a recovery CTA
heuristics.trigger: Any screen that can show an error state — form submission, data load, action confirmation, payment processing.
heuristics.check: Does every error state in the design include explicit CTAs telling the user what to do next — retry, edit, go back, contact support? Or does the error just state what went wrong with no action?
heuristics.good_example: Payment-error frame includes: 'We couldn't process your payment. Please check your card details and try again.' [Try Again] [Use Different Card] [Contact Support].
heuristics.bad_example: Error state shows 'Payment failed. Error code 5023.' with no buttons or links — user has nowhere to go.

heuristics.title: Error placement designed at the right scope
heuristics.trigger: A screen has forms, multi-step flows, or actions that can fail at different scopes (single field, whole form, whole page, single component on a larger page).
heuristics.check: Are error states designed at the appropriate scope — field-level errors next to the field, form-level errors at the form, page-level errors when the entire page can't load, component-level errors confined to the component?
heuristics.good_example: Form design shows inline field-level errors under each field, a form-level error banner at the top of the form for server rejections, and a separate full-page error state.
heuristics.bad_example: Only one error pattern is designed — a full-width red banner — used regardless of whether one field failed or the whole page broke.

heuristics.title: Distinct designed states for different error causes
heuristics.trigger: A screen makes server requests that can fail for distinguishable reasons — network, server outage, user permission, validation.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn distinct states for errors the user can fix (validation, expired session, bad input) vs. errors they can't (server down, network gone)? Or is there a single generic 'something went wrong' frame?
heuristics.good_example: Three distinct frames in the file: offline ('You are offline — changes will sync when you reconnect'), server-down ('Our servers are temporarily unreachable'), validation ('Please correct the highlighted fields').
heuristics.bad_example: A single 'Something went wrong, please try again' error frame used for every failure mode.

heuristics.title: Designed error state shows the form with user input intact
heuristics.trigger: A form submission can fail — validation rejection, server error, network loss.
heuristics.check: When the designer drew the error state, does the form still show the user's input filled in (not blank)? Designing the error frame with empty fields signals to engineering that resetting is fine.
heuristics.good_example: Error-state mockup of a signup form shows the email field populated with 'theo@example.com', the password field shown as filled, with the error banner above. Engineering knows to preserve input.
heuristics.bad_example: Error-state frame shows an empty form with the error banner — engineering interprets this as 'clear the form on error', losing user input.

heuristics.title: Designed re-auth modal + return-state for session expiry
heuristics.trigger: A screen has actions that require an authenticated session and the user may be active for long periods — drafts, forms, editors, multi-step flows.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn (a) the in-context re-auth modal that appears when a session expires mid-action, and (b) the post-reauth return state showing the user's work intact? Or is session expiry undesigned, defaulting to a redirect?
heuristics.good_example: File includes: session-expired modal 'Please sign back in to save', and a return-state frame showing the editor with the draft visibly preserved after re-auth.
heuristics.bad_example: Session expiry isn't designed — engineering defaults to a redirect to the login page, and the user lands on the dashboard with their work gone.

heuristics.title: Designed state for logged-out access to protected screens
heuristics.trigger: A screen requires authentication to be useful — account, settings, dashboard, personal content.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn what a non-authenticated user sees when they land on this URL? Sign-in prompt with context, and a return path after auth?
heuristics.good_example: Logged-out /account frame: 'Sign in to view your account' [Sign In] [Create Account]. PRD specifies that after sign-in the user returns to /account.
heuristics.bad_example: Logged-out access to protected screens isn't designed — engineering picks a default (redirect to home, generic error) and the user's intent is lost.

heuristics.title: Designed treatment for actions the user can see but can't perform
heuristics.trigger: A screen shows actions/controls (buttons, menus, links) whose availability depends on the user's role or permissions.
heuristics.check: Has the designer chosen and drawn how unauthorized actions appear — hidden, disabled-with-tooltip-explanation, or shown-then-rejected-on-click? Or is the permission case undesigned, leaving engineering to pick?
heuristics.good_example: Design includes the 'Delete project' button in a viewer-role variant: grayed out with a tooltip on hover 'Only project owners can delete projects.'
heuristics.bad_example: Only the owner-role variant of each action is designed. The viewer-role state isn't shown — engineering ships an active button that errors on click.

heuristics.title: Designed re-auth gate for sensitive actions
heuristics.trigger: A screen exposes destructive or security-relevant actions — delete account, change password, change billing method, transfer ownership.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn the re-auth step (password confirm, 2FA challenge) before the destructive action, even though the user is already signed in? Or does the destructive action lead directly to the consequence with only a generic confirm?
heuristics.good_example: Delete-account flow in the file includes a re-auth modal asking the user to re-type their password before the deletion is committed.
heuristics.bad_example: Destructive action flow goes straight from button → 'Are you sure?' → done. No re-auth designed.

heuristics.title: Designed state for server-side validation rejection
heuristics.trigger: A form with client-side validation submits data to a server — signup, profile update, content creation, payment.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn the post-submit state for when the server rejects something client-side validation can't catch (username taken, email already in use, payment declined, policy violation)?
heuristics.good_example: Signup form has a designed state showing 'This email is already in use' appearing next to the email field after submit, distinct from format errors.
heuristics.bad_example: Only client-side error states are designed. Server-only rejection cases aren't shown — engineering improvises a generic banner.

heuristics.title: Designed format hints before the user errors
heuristics.trigger: A field requires a specific format — phone, date, password complexity, ID number.
heuristics.check: Has the designer included visible format hints in the field's default state — helper text, placeholder, or a live rules list — so users see expectations before making a mistake?
heuristics.good_example: Password field has a designed below-field rules list visible from focus: 'At least 8 characters / One number / One special character', with check/cross icons that respond to typing.
heuristics.bad_example: Field shows no format hint by default. Format expectations only appear in the error state, after the user has already failed.

heuristics.title: Designed loading / success / error states for async field checks
heuristics.trigger: A field's validity requires a server check — username uniqueness, coupon validity, address verification, domain availability.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn the three states the field needs — checking (spinner), available (success indicator), unavailable (error + ideally a suggested alternative)?
heuristics.good_example: Username field design includes all three states: small spinner while checking, '✓ Available' on success, '✗ Taken — try "theo.designs2"' on failure with the alternative auto-populated.
heuristics.bad_example: Only the default field state is designed. The checking / available / unavailable states aren't drawn — engineering invents them.

heuristics.title: Required vs. optional fields are visually distinguished
heuristics.trigger: A form has multiple fields where some are required and some are optional.
heuristics.check: Has the designer specified a clear, consistent convention for distinguishing required from optional fields — asterisk markers, 'Optional' labels, a legend, or some equivalent? Is the convention applied uniformly across the form?
heuristics.good_example: Required fields are marked with a red asterisk; a legend at the top of the form reads '* required'. Optional fields are unmarked. Convention is consistent throughout.
heuristics.bad_example: All fields look identical — no asterisks, no 'Optional' tags, no helper text. Users only learn which fields were required after submitting and getting an error.

heuristics.title: Designed offline state
heuristics.trigger: A screen depends on live data or remote actions to function.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn what the screen looks like when the device goes offline? Offline banner, indication of what still works, and (if applicable) the 'queued for sync' visual for user actions?
heuristics.good_example: Offline-state mockup shows a non-blocking banner 'You're offline — new messages will be sent when you reconnect', already-loaded content still visible, send button changed to a queued-clock icon.
heuristics.bad_example: No offline state designed. Engineering ships generic 'failed to fetch' errors and the user can't tell their connection is the problem.

heuristics.title: Designed slow-network state distinct from offline
heuristics.trigger: A screen depends on data that may load slowly on weak connections — large lists, image-heavy content, video, file uploads.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn the 'online but slow' state — long-loading placeholders, low-res image previews that resolve, 'this is taking longer than usual' messaging? Distinct from a full offline state?
heuristics.good_example: Image-heavy feed design includes a low-res-placeholder state for slow-loading images, and a 'This is taking longer than usual' message that appears after 8 seconds.
heuristics.bad_example: Slow-connection state isn't designed. It looks identical to a fast load (just longer), leaving users uncertain whether they're frozen or offline.

heuristics.title: Designed timeout state with retry/cancel
heuristics.trigger: A screen makes server requests that could hang or take very long.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn what the user sees when a request hangs past a reasonable threshold (10–30s)? Is there a designed timeout state with [Keep waiting] [Retry] [Cancel] options?
heuristics.good_example: Timeout-state frame shows: 'This is taking longer than usual.' with three explicit buttons [Keep waiting] [Retry] [Cancel].
heuristics.bad_example: No timeout state designed. The loading state in the file has no escape hatch — engineering ships a spinner that spins forever.

heuristics.title: Designed retry affordance after failure
heuristics.trigger: A screen can fail to load or to complete an action because of transient network/server issues.
heuristics.check: Does the failure state include a designed retry button positioned where content would have appeared? Or does the failure state expect the user to refresh the whole page?
heuristics.good_example: Failed-feed-load state shows: 'Couldn't load your feed.' with a prominent [Retry] button in the content area.
heuristics.bad_example: Failure state is just an error message — no retry button. Engineering's only option is to require a full page refresh.

heuristics.title: Design demonstrates overflow handling with realistic long content
heuristics.trigger: A screen displays user- or system-generated text in constrained spaces — titles, names, file names, descriptions, labels.
heuristics.check: Has the designer mocked at least one example with text well beyond the design's assumed length to demonstrate the truncation, wrap, or expand behavior?
heuristics.good_example: Card grid in the design file shows a mix of short and very long titles — long titles truncate at 2 lines with ellipsis, full title appears on hover.
heuristics.bad_example: All mocked cards use short, neat titles. Overflow behavior is undefined — engineering picks (often: layout breaks).

heuristics.title: Designed treatment for missing optional fields
heuristics.trigger: A screen renders content with multiple fields where some may be optional or unset — profile bio, project description, avatar, secondary metadata.
heuristics.check: Has the designer mocked a variant of the screen where optional fields are empty/null, showing what each empty field looks like — collapsed, placeholder, hidden?
heuristics.good_example: Profile design includes a variant: user with no bio, no website, default avatar. The bio section is shown either as 'Add a bio' (owner-view) or omitted entirely (visitor-view).
heuristics.bad_example: Only the fully-populated profile is mocked. The empty-fields variant is undesigned — engineering may ship 'null' strings or empty label rows.

heuristics.title: Design shows large-number formatting
heuristics.trigger: A screen displays numeric values that could grow large — counts (likes, views, comments), prices, durations, file sizes.
heuristics.check: Has the designer specified how large numbers are formatted in the design (e.g. '2.5M', '1.2K') and shown at least one mock with a large value?
heuristics.good_example: Post card design shows a mock with '2.5M views' alongside '47 views', demonstrating the formatting threshold and how it renders.
heuristics.bad_example: All mocked counts are small (12, 47, 134). Large-number formatting is unspecified — engineering picks (often: raw integers that break layout).

heuristics.title: Design proofed at expanded/RTL text variants
heuristics.trigger: The product is intended for international users / the PRD mentions localization.
heuristics.check: Has the designer included a variant of key screens with translated labels at ~30–40% expansion and/or an RTL variant?
heuristics.good_example: Design file includes the primary screens in English, German (showing button labels and headers at expanded width), and Arabic (RTL mirrored).
heuristics.bad_example: Only English mocks in the file. Internationalization is a stated requirement but no proof exists that the layout holds.
heuristics.notes: Skip if PRD doesn't indicate international plans.

heuristics.title: Designed conflict-resolution state for stale edits
heuristics.trigger: A screen lets the user edit content that could have been modified by another user, another session, or a background process since the screen loaded.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn the conflict-resolution UI for when the user tries to save changes to data that's been updated server-side?
heuristics.good_example: Conflict-resolution frame: 'This project was updated by Sarah 5 minutes ago.' [View their changes] [Overwrite] [Discard mine].
heuristics.bad_example: No conflict state designed. The save either silently overwrites or fails with a cryptic 'conflict error' from engineering's default error path.

heuristics.title: Designed disabled state for actions dependent on loading data
heuristics.trigger: A screen loads data that affects what actions are valid — a list before bulk operations, item details before edit, account state before payment.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn what the dependent actions look like while their underlying data is still loading?
heuristics.good_example: Bulk-edit toolbar is shown in two states in the design: enabled (after list loads) and disabled-while-loading with a 'Loading items…' tooltip.
heuristics.bad_example: Only the post-load state of the toolbar is designed — the pre-load state is unspecified, so engineering enables actions immediately and the user can act on stale state.

heuristics.title: Designed undo affordance for destructive actions
heuristics.trigger: A screen offers actions that delete, remove, archive, or permanently change user data — and the action is not strictly irreversible.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn the undo affordance that appears after the destructive action — a toast with an [Undo] button or equivalent persistent recovery?
heuristics.good_example: Delete-email flow in the design shows a toast appearing after deletion: 'Email moved to Trash. [Undo]' that persists ~5 seconds.
heuristics.bad_example: Destructive action flow goes through a confirmation modal but no undo state is designed. Once confirmed, recovery isn't shown — engineering ships permanent deletion with no fallback.

heuristics.title: Designed proportional confirmation for irreversible actions
heuristics.trigger: A screen offers actions that are genuinely irreversible — account deletion, permanent data wipe, immutable commits.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn an explicit confirmation that demonstrates intent (type a phrase, re-enter password, multi-step), proportional to the consequence?
heuristics.good_example: Delete-account flow includes a designed modal requiring the user to type their account email; the delete button is shown in a disabled state until typed email matches.
heuristics.bad_example: Account deletion is a single 'Delete account' button → 'Are you sure?' → done. The proportional friction is undesigned.

heuristics.title: Designed save-state indicator for long-form input
heuristics.trigger: A screen has multi-field or long-text input where users can spend significant time before submitting — composer, editor, multi-step form, document.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn a visible save-state indicator (e.g. 'Saved 5 seconds ago', 'Saving…', 'Unsaved changes')?
heuristics.good_example: Editor design shows three indicator states near the title: 'Saved', 'Saving…' (with subtle spinner), 'Unsaved changes' (subtle warning color).
heuristics.bad_example: No save indicator designed. Even if auto-save is implemented, users have no visible signal — they don't trust it, or worse, don't realize they can close safely.

heuristics.title: Error states use more than color
heuristics.trigger: A screen has error states on fields, banners, or status indicators.
heuristics.check: Does the designed error state combine multiple signals — color + icon + text? Or is the error conveyed by color alone?
heuristics.good_example: Designed invalid-email state: red border + warning icon + 'Please enter a valid email' helper text. Three reinforcing signals.
heuristics.bad_example: Designed error relies only on a red border around the field — no icon, no text. Invisible to red-green color-blind users.

heuristics.title: Touch targets sized for the mobile breakpoint
heuristics.trigger: The design includes a mobile / narrow-viewport breakpoint where elements will be tapped on touch devices.
heuristics.check: Are interactive elements at the mobile breakpoint at least 44×44px in size (or padded to that), with enough separation from adjacent targets to avoid mis-taps?
heuristics.good_example: Mobile breakpoint design shows icon-only buttons in the nav at 48×48px with 8px of separation between them.
heuristics.bad_example: Mobile breakpoint preserves desktop 16px icon buttons stacked tightly — tap targets too small and too close.

heuristics.title: Copy variants designed for singular and plural counts
heuristics.trigger: A screen shows counts that drive copy — '1 item / 3 items', '0 results / 1 result / 12 results'.
heuristics.check: Has the designer specified copy variants for singular vs. plural (and ideally for zero)?
heuristics.good_example: Selection bar design includes three variants: '0 selected' (disabled state), '1 file selected', '2 files selected'.
heuristics.bad_example: Only '5 files selected' is mocked. The singular case is unspecified — engineering ships '1 files'.

heuristics.title: Designed treatment for unbounded counts
heuristics.trigger: A screen displays collections that can grow unbounded — notifications, search results, history, files, messages.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn how the design holds at high counts? Pagination, '99+' truncation, 'load more' / 'show all 1,234' affordance?
heuristics.good_example: Notification badge design includes a variant showing '99+' for counts over 99. List design shows 25-item pagination with explicit 'page X of Y' controls.
heuristics.bad_example: Badge mock shows '3 unread' — but no variant at 200, 2000, or 20000. Engineering picks (often: raw number, breaking the badge).

heuristics.title: Designed treatment for the single-item case in collection layouts
heuristics.trigger: A screen uses list, grid, carousel, or comparison layouts to display content.
heuristics.check: Has the designer mocked the layout with exactly one item to verify it doesn't look broken?
heuristics.good_example: Two-up comparison design includes a one-item variant that hides the second panel and reflows to a single full-width card.
heuristics.bad_example: Only multi-item states mocked. Single-item case is undesigned — engineering ships a four-column grid with one card stranded in the top-left.

heuristics.title: Designed post-success state for completed actions
heuristics.trigger: A screen has a primary action whose success has consequences worth confirming — submission, payment, account creation, content publishing, file save, item added.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn what the user sees AFTER the action succeeds?
heuristics.good_example: Checkout flow ends with a designed confirmation screen: order number, summary, expected delivery, next steps. Email confirmation visual is also drawn.
heuristics.bad_example: Form submit is mocked, but what happens after success isn't. Engineering ships a brief toast and dumps the user back at the dashboard.
heuristics.notes: One of the most common gaps. Designers design the action up to submit and skip what comes after.

heuristics.title: Designed disabled state for primary actions
heuristics.trigger: A screen has primary CTAs (Submit, Save, Send, Pay, Continue) whose availability depends on prerequisites.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn the disabled state of the primary action, and is it visually distinct from the active state? Is it clear what the user needs to do to enable it?
heuristics.good_example: Checkout design shows 'Pay' in two states: disabled (grayed, with hover tooltip 'Add a shipping address to continue') and active (full color, hover style).
heuristics.bad_example: Primary CTA only drawn in its active state. The disabled case isn't mocked — engineering picks a disabled visual that may look indistinguishable from active.

heuristics.title: Designed selected/active state for interactive items
heuristics.trigger: A screen has lists, tables, sidebars, tabs, or grids where the user can select or navigate to a specific item, and the selection has visible consequence.
heuristics.check: Has the designer drawn the selected/active state of items in the list, distinct from default and hover?
heuristics.good_example: Sidebar nav design shows the active page item with a different background, a left-edge accent bar, and bolder text — clearly distinct from default and hover.
heuristics.bad_example: Only the default state of nav items is drawn. The active/selected state isn't specified — engineering picks a subtle change (or none).
heuristics.notes: Especially common gap in tables, sidebars, and master-detail views.

heuristics.title: Primary subject identity is visible and prominent
heuristics.trigger: A screen presents a specific piece of content as its subject — a recipe, product, article, profile, item detail, document.
heuristics.check: Is the content's primary identifier (name, title, headline) visible, prominently sized, and positioned where the eye lands first? Or is the subject's identity absent or buried?
heuristics.good_example: Recipe detail screen leads with the dish name as a large heading above the image, immediately answering 'what am I looking at?'
heuristics.bad_example: Recipe screen shows ingredients, cooking steps, and a photo, but no visible dish name — the subject's identity is missing.
heuristics.notes: Phrased as question because the absence may be intentional (brand minimalism, hover-reveal). Opens dialogue rather than assuming oversight.

heuristics.title: One primary action is visually dominant
heuristics.trigger: A screen has multiple interactive actions visible in its primary interaction area (toolbar, action bar, header).
heuristics.check: Is exactly one action visually dominant as THE primary action — distinct fill, color, weight? Or do multiple actions compete with similar visual weight?
heuristics.good_example: An action bar has 'Cook' as the only filled branded button; Save and Watch are outline-styled, clearly secondary.
heuristics.bad_example: Three buttons of similar weight, color, and size sit side-by-side — user has no clear signal which is the primary action.
heuristics.notes: Can be deliberate flat hierarchy in some product contexts. Question framing surfaces it without assuming oversight.

heuristics.title: First viewport delivers the screen's primary value
heuristics.trigger: A screen has a clear primary purpose (browse, buy, sign up, read, configure) and content that extends beyond the first viewport.
heuristics.check: Within the first viewport (above the fold), does the user see what they came for — primary identity, key supporting info, and primary action? Or does the user need to scroll to find why they're on this screen?
heuristics.good_example: A product page shows the product name, image, price, key specs, and 'Add to cart' button all above the fold — the user can evaluate and act without scrolling.
heuristics.bad_example: A recipe page above the fold shows only the nav and the hero photo — the dish name, prep time, servings, and 'Cook' button all require scrolling.
heuristics.notes: What 'above the fold' means depends on viewport. If both desktop and mobile breakpoints are designed, flag based on the smaller of the two.

heuristics.title: Interactive elements signal interactivity
heuristics.trigger: A screen contains elements that respond to user action — buttons, links, tappable cards, scannable codes, dismissible elements, expandable areas.
heuristics.check: Does each interactive element have a visible signal of interactivity — button styling, icon, label, hover-state hint? Or do interactive elements visually present as static decoration?
heuristics.good_example: A QR code in the corner has a 'Scan' label and a subtle button frame — clearly actionable.
heuristics.bad_example: A QR code sits in the corner with no label, no border, no signal of what it does or whether to interact with it.
heuristics.notes: Common gap on dense screens where designers assume context will make interactivity obvious.

heuristics.title: Same element types treated identically
heuristics.trigger: A screen displays multiple instances of the same type of element — ingredient cards, product tiles, list items, avatars, thumbnails.
heuristics.check: Are all instances of the same type rendered identically — shape, fill, content slots, including the edge case where source data is missing? Or do some instances visually deviate (placeholder text instead of an image, different alignment, missing components)?
heuristics.good_example: All ingredient cards in a recipe show a circular thumbnail; for an ingredient without a photo, a stylized icon fills the same circle so the grid stays visually consistent.
heuristics.bad_example: 13 ingredient cards show photographs; one shows 'GY' placeholder text — the inconsistency reads as broken or unfinished rather than intentional.
heuristics.notes: When a single instance deviates from the pattern, it's almost always an unintentional gap — hence default gap framing.

heuristics.title: Typography and spacing consistent within the screen
heuristics.trigger: A screen contains multiple text elements at different roles (headings, body, labels, metadata).
heuristics.check: Is the typographic scale and spacing system applied consistently across the screen, or do similar-role elements use inconsistent sizes, weights, or rhythms?
heuristics.good_example: All section headers use the same scale; all metadata labels use a consistent smaller size; spacing between sections follows a clear rhythm.
heuristics.bad_example: Section headers vary in size between sections; metadata labels inconsistently use 12px and 14px; section spacing alternates between 16px and 32px with no clear pattern.

heuristics.title: Metadata needed to evaluate the content is present
heuristics.trigger: A screen presents an item whose value depends on contextual data — a recipe, product, article, event, listing, profile.
heuristics.check: Is the metadata a user would need to evaluate or use the content prominently shown — time, servings, difficulty for a recipe; price, stock, shipping for a product; date, author, read-time for an article?
heuristics.good_example: Recipe detail shows under the title: '30 min · serves 4 · easy · vegetarian' — at-a-glance evaluation data immediately visible.
heuristics.bad_example: Recipe detail shows ingredients and steps but no time, servings, or difficulty visible without exploring further.

heuristics.title: Trust and quality signals where contextually warranted
heuristics.trigger: A screen presents content whose credibility or quality affects user decisions — a recipe, product, article, profile, listing, professional service.
heuristics.check: Is there a designed signal of trustworthiness — rating, review count, source attribution, professional credential, 'verified by' badge? Or is the content presented with no quality signals at all?
heuristics.good_example: Recipe shows '★ 4.8 (1,247 reviews) — by Chef Julia Mendez' near the title.
heuristics.bad_example: Recipe content has no rating, no review count, no author attribution — user has no shortcut to evaluate trust.
heuristics.notes: Can be a deliberate brand decision (premium curation implies trust without ratings). Question framing surfaces it without judgment.

heuristics.title: Density appropriate for the content type and user task
heuristics.trigger: A screen presents multiple sections of content simultaneously.
heuristics.check: Is the visual density appropriate for the user's task — scannable for browsing, focused for action? Or does the screen overwhelm with too much simultaneous information / too little whitespace?
heuristics.good_example: A recipe screen balances generous whitespace around primary content with denser secondary content — the eye knows where to rest and where to scan.
heuristics.bad_example: Every section of the screen competes equally for attention with similar density throughout — user doesn't know where to start.

heuristics.title: Current mode or context is visibly indicated
heuristics.trigger: A screen supports multiple modes, contexts, or user states (browse vs. cook; admin vs. member; edit vs. view; logged-in vs. preview).
heuristics.check: Is the current mode/context visibly indicated so the user can tell what state they're in? Or does the same screen appear identical across modes, leaving the user to infer?
heuristics.good_example: Cooking mode shows a 'Cooking' pill in the header with a colored dot, dimming non-essential UI; browse mode shows the full nav.
heuristics.bad_example: Cook mode and browse mode look identical except for a small button label change; user has to guess what they're in.

heuristics.title: Elements don't unintentionally overlap or clip
heuristics.trigger: Any designed screen.
heuristics.check: Do any elements visibly overlap, clip, or obscure other content in ways that look unintended — floating bars covering scrollable content, modals partially off-screen, tooltips clipped by container edges?
heuristics.good_example: Floating action bar maintains sufficient bottom padding on the scroll content so the last item is fully visible without scrolling beyond.
heuristics.bad_example: A floating action bar partially covers content underneath it — content peeks through, suggesting layout integrity wasn't checked.

heuristics.title: Each step follows naturally from the previous
heuristics.trigger: Two or more screens uploaded representing a sequence (steps in a flow, not standalone variants).
heuristics.check: Do the screens form a coherent sequence where each step follows naturally from the previous — context preserved, state carried, transition explained? Or is there a visible gap (jump in state, missing intermediate step)?
heuristics.good_example: A checkout flow shows Cart → Address → Payment → Confirmation, each step naturally following from the last with state carried through.
heuristics.bad_example: Screen 1 shows 'Add to cart'; Screen 3 shows 'Order confirmation'. The expected intermediate step (cart review or checkout form) is missing from the uploaded flow.

heuristics.title: Back and cancel paths visible at every step
heuristics.trigger: Two or more screens in a flow.
heuristics.check: At each step in the flow, is there a visible affordance to go back to the previous step or cancel out of the flow entirely? Or does the user appear trapped after a certain step?
heuristics.good_example: Each step in a multi-step checkout has a 'Back' link at top-left and a 'Cancel order' option in the secondary actions.
heuristics.bad_example: Screens 2 and 3 have no visible back or cancel affordance — once the user reaches step 2, they appear to be trapped in the flow.

heuristics.title: User input or selection persists visibly across screens
heuristics.trigger: A flow where user input or selection on one screen should be visible on subsequent screens — form → confirmation, search → results, selection → detail, configuration → summary.
heuristics.check: Does the design show the user's input or selection visibly persisting on later screens — entered email shown in confirmation, selected item displayed on detail, search term echoed in results header?
heuristics.good_example: Checkout confirmation displays the email entered during signup, the items selected in the cart, and the shipping address chosen on the previous step.
heuristics.bad_example: User enters an email during signup; the confirmation screen shows generic 'Thanks for signing up' with no echo of the email or what was just done.

heuristics.title: Visual system consistent across the flow
heuristics.trigger: Two or more screens in a flow.
heuristics.check: Are typographic scale, spacing patterns, button styles, and component patterns consistent across all screens in the flow? Or do they diverge in ways that look unintentional?
heuristics.good_example: All screens in a flow share the same typographic scale, button styles, and component patterns — the flow feels like one coherent design.
heuristics.bad_example: Screens 1 and 2 use a 16px body / 24px heading scale with rounded buttons; screen 3 uses 14px / 20px and square buttons. The inconsistency suggests different sources or unfinished design.
heuristics.notes: Can be intentional (different brand zones), but usually surfaces real handoff gaps.

heuristics.title: Clear entry and exit/completion states designed
heuristics.trigger: A flow representing a task with a beginning and an end.
heuristics.check: Does the flow have a clearly designed entry point (where the user comes from, what triggers the flow) and an exit/completion state (where the user goes after success)?
heuristics.good_example: Checkout flow starts from a 'Start checkout' button on the cart screen and ends with a confirmation screen showing order details and a 'Continue shopping' or 'Track order' next-step CTA.
heuristics.bad_example: Flow screens begin mid-action with no apparent entry trigger, and the last screen shows the submitted form fading away with no completion state or next-step guidance.

heuristics.title: User's position in the flow is visible at every step
heuristics.trigger: A flow of three or more steps representing a structured sequence (onboarding, checkout, multi-step form, wizard, signup).
heuristics.check: Does every screen in the flow show the user where they are — step counter, progress bar, breadcrumbs, named-step indicator? Or do steps look isolated, leaving the user uncertain how much more there is?
heuristics.good_example: Checkout shows '2 of 4 · Shipping' with a progress bar at the top of every step. The user always knows what's remaining.
heuristics.bad_example: Each step in an onboarding flow shows only its own content with no indicator of step number, total count, or progress. The user can't tell if they're nearly done or just starting.

heuristics.title: All PRD-stated features have a corresponding designed element
heuristics.trigger: The PRD or context lists specific features, capabilities, or requirements that should be in the design.
heuristics.check: For each PRD-stated feature, is there a screen or designed element that addresses it? Or are there stated requirements with no visible design counterpart in the uploaded screens?
heuristics.good_example: PRD specifies 'guest checkout', 'saved addresses', and 'order tracking'. All three appear as designed screens or visible elements across the flow.
heuristics.bad_example: PRD specifies 'guest checkout' as a required feature, but the uploaded screens only show authenticated-user checkout flows — no guest path is mocked.

heuristics.title: Design doesn't contradict explicit PRD claims
heuristics.trigger: The PRD makes specific claims about UX, behavior, or capabilities ('single-tap actions', 'no required signup', 'works offline', 'free first audit').
heuristics.check: Does the design contradict any of these claims? Look for cases where the designed interaction is more complex, restrictive, or different than the PRD promises.
heuristics.good_example: PRD says 'no signup required for first audit'. The design shows the audit flow accessible without any signup gate.
heuristics.bad_example: PRD says 'no signup required for first audit'. The audit page in the design shows a 'Sign up to continue' gate before the first audit can be run — direct contradiction.

heuristics.title: Design supports stated user goals or success criteria
heuristics.trigger: The PRD describes specific user goals or success criteria ('users complete onboarding in <2 minutes', 'find a recipe in under 30 seconds').
heuristics.check: Does the design serve the stated goal? Does flow length, primary action visibility, and information density align with the goal — or does the design impose more friction than the stated goal allows?
heuristics.good_example: PRD goal: 'complete signup in <60 seconds.' Designed signup is one screen with two required fields and clear primary CTA — aligned with the goal.
heuristics.bad_example: PRD goal: 'complete signup in <60 seconds.' Designed signup is 5 screens deep with optional fields presented as required and a non-prominent 'Continue' action — design imposes friction the goal can't tolerate.

heuristics.title: PRD's primary user journey fully represented in screens
heuristics.trigger: The PRD describes a primary user journey or sequence of user actions ('user discovers a recipe, saves it, cooks it later').
heuristics.check: Is the entire described journey represented across the uploaded screens? Or are critical steps in the stated journey missing from the design?
heuristics.good_example: PRD describes 'discover → save → cook' as the primary journey. Uploaded screens include a Discover page, a Save action with a Saved Recipes view, and a Cook mode — full journey covered.
heuristics.bad_example: PRD describes 'discover → save → cook' as the primary journey. Uploaded screens include Discover and Cook, but no Save / Saved Recipes view — middle of the journey missing.
heuristics.notes: Phrased as question because the missing screens may exist but not have been uploaded.

heuristics.title: PRD-stated constraints visible in the design
heuristics.trigger: The PRD states constraints — 'must work on mobile', 'WCAG AA accessible', 'works offline', 'no third-party dependencies', 'PCI-compliant payment'.
heuristics.check: Does the design visibly respect each stated constraint? Or does the design fail to demonstrate compliance with a stated constraint?
heuristics.good_example: PRD: 'mobile-first design.' Uploaded screens include both desktop and mobile breakpoints, with mobile shown as the primary canvas.
heuristics.bad_example: PRD: 'mobile-first design.' All uploaded screens are desktop views with no mobile breakpoint shown — the constraint isn't demonstrated.

heuristics.title: All PRD-mentioned user types or roles addressed by the design
heuristics.trigger: The PRD identifies multiple user types, roles, or personas ('admin / member / viewer', 'first-time user / returning user', 'free tier / pro tier').
heuristics.check: Are all PRD-mentioned user types represented in the design — either with distinct screens or with clearly designed role variants? Or does the design only address one of the stated user types?
heuristics.good_example: PRD identifies 'free tier' and 'pro tier' users. Design includes variants of key screens showing how each tier sees the product — gated features, upsell prompts, full access.
heuristics.bad_example: PRD identifies 'admin' and 'viewer' roles with different permissions. Design only shows the admin experience — no viewer-role variants exist for screens where permissions matter.
